A.explanation: Two equal forces in the same direction add to a resultant of $2F$, so the body would accelerate and this is not a couple.

B.explanation: Equal and opposite forces cancel to zero resultant force, but separation between the lines gives a resultant moment $F \times d$.

C.explanation: A couple has no resultant force but it must have a resultant moment, otherwise it would have no turning effect.

D.explanation: Unequal opposite forces on the same line leave a non-zero resultant force and have no perpendicular separation, so no couple moment.

hints: Look at each option for two details: whether the two forces are equal and opposite, and whether they act along the same line or different lines.
Recall that a couple must give zero resultant force for translation but a non-zero turning effect from the separation $d$ between the lines of action.
Check which pair cancels as vectors yet still produces moment $F \times d$, and reject any pair that leaves a resultant force or gives no moment.
walkthrough: Identify what is tested: the definition of a couple as a special pair of forces acting on a body.
State the first condition: the forces must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so vector sum is zero and there is no resultant force.
State the second condition: the forces must act along different parallel lines, so the perpendicular distance $d$ between them gives a resultant moment of $F \times d$.
Compare the options: same-direction forces leave a resultant, no moment means no turning effect, and same-line forces cannot form a separated pair.
Only the pair that is equal and opposite but separated satisfies both zero resultant force and non-zero resultant moment. This is option B.
